lead: The Brayton cycle (also called the Joule cycle) is the ideal cycle of the gas turbine: air is compressed, heated at constant pressure, expanded through a turbine and cooled at constant pressure. It runs in steady flow, so its key number is the pressure ratio, not a volume ratio. It models aircraft jet engines and the gas turbines of power stations. The Stirling cycle is a piston cycle with two isothermal and two constant-volume processes and a regenerator that stores heat inside the engine. With a perfect regenerator it reaches the Carnot efficiency, which is why it is studied for solar-dish and other external-heat engines.
prereq: You need the process relations from Air standard cycles and their assumptions and the steady flow energy equation from the topic Steady flow energy equation and its applications.

blocks.text: State 1 is the compressor inlet. The processes are 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 heat addition at constant pressure (the combustor), 3→4 isentropic expansion in the turbine and 4→1 heat rejection at constant pressure. In a real open-cycle gas turbine, fresh air enters and exhaust leaves; the closed air standard cycle replaces the combustor by a heater and the atmosphere by a cooler.

The pressure ratio is rp = p₂/p₁ = p₃/p₄. Both isentropic steps work across it, so T₂/T₁ = T₃/T₄ = rp(γ−1)/γ. Each device is a steady-flow device, and the steady flow energy equation gives, per kg of air:

items: compressor work w<sub>c</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₂ − T₁); turbine work w<sub>t</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₃ − T₄);
heat added q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₃ − T₂); net work w<sub>net</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − w<sub>c</sub>;
ηBrayton = 1 − 1/rp(γ−1)/γ, and the back work ratio wc/wt.

blocks.text: The efficiency formula looks like the Otto formula with rγ−1 replaced by rp(γ−1)/γ. It depends only on the pressure ratio. The back work ratio is large in a gas turbine (often 40 to 60% of the turbine work drives the compressor), so small losses in the compressor and turbine cut the net work sharply.

sections.h3: Pressure ratio for maximum net work

blocks.text: For fixed T₁ and T₃ (the turbine inlet temperature is limited by the blade material), η keeps rising with r<sub>p</sub>, but the net work does not. At r<sub>p</sub> = 1 nothing is compressed; at the r<sub>p</sub> where T₂ reaches T₃ no heat can be added. Between them w<sub>net</sub> has a maximum. Writing x = r<sub>p</sub><sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>, w<sub>net</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>[T₃(1 − 1/x) − T₁(x − 1)], and dw<sub>net</sub>/dx = 0 gives x = √(T₃/T₁). So
The table is for T₁ = 300 K and T₃ = 1200 K. Past the optimum, the efficiency still rises but each kg of air gives less work, so the engine must be larger for the same power.

With state 1 the start of compression at the largest volume, the processes are 1→2 isothermal compression at T<sub>L</sub> (heat rejected), 2→3 heating at constant volume, 3→4 isothermal expansion at T<sub>H</sub> (heat added) and 4→1 cooling at constant volume. The two constant-volume steps exchange the same amount of heat, c<sub>v</sub>(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub>).

The regenerator is a matrix of fine wire or metal mesh between the hot and cold spaces. In 4→1 the gas gives its heat to the matrix; in 2→3 the gas takes the same heat back. With a perfect regenerator, outside heat enters only at TH and leaves only at TL, so
ηStirling = R(TH − TL) ln r / [RTH ln r] = 1 − TL/TH, where r = v₁/v₂.

Without a regenerator the heat for 2→3 must come from outside too, and the efficiency drops far below Carnot. The Ericsson cycle is the same idea with two constant-pressure steps instead of constant-volume ones; it too reaches the Carnot efficiency with perfect regeneration.

examples.question: An ideal Brayton cycle has a pressure ratio of 8. Air enters the compressor at 300 K and the turbine at 1200 K. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find the compressor and turbine work, the net work, the heat added, the efficiency and the back work ratio. Then find the pressure ratio that gives the most net work and that work.
steps: Back work ratio = 244.7/540.2 = 0.453: 45% of the turbine work drives the compressor.
examples.answer: w<sub>c</sub> = 244.7 kJ/kg, w<sub>t</sub> = 540.2 kJ/kg, w<sub>net</sub> = 295.6 kJ/kg, q<sub>in</sub> = 659.8 kJ/kg, η = 44.8%, back work ratio 0.453; r<sub>p,opt</sub> = 11.31 with w<sub>max</sub> = 301.5 kJ/kg.

examples.question: A Stirling engine uses air between 300 K and 900 K with a volume ratio v₁/v₂ = 2; at state 1 (largest volume, 300 K) the pressure is 1 bar. Find the pressures, the net work and the efficiency (a) with a perfect regenerator, (b) with no regenerator, (c) with a regenerator that recovers 80% of the constant-volume heat. R = 0.287 and c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K.
steps: Pressures: p₂ = 2 bar (isothermal, half the volume), p₃ = 2 × 900/300 = 6 bar, p₄ = 6/2 = 3 bar.
Net work = R(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub>) ln 2 = 0.287 × 600 × 0.6931 = 119.4 kJ/kg.
Heat in at T<sub>H</sub>: 0.287 × 900 × 0.6931 = 179.0 kJ/kg. Constant-volume heat: 0.718 × 600 = 430.8 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: p₂ = 2 bar, p₃ = 6 bar, p₄ = 3 bar; w<sub>net</sub> = 119.4 kJ/kg; η = 66.7% with a perfect regenerator, 19.6% with none, 45.0% at 80% recovery. The regenerator is what makes the Stirling engine worth building.

traps: The Brayton formula uses r<sub>p</sub><sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>, not r<sub>p</sub><sup>γ−1</sup>. Using the wrong exponent at r<sub>p</sub> = 8 gives 1 − 1/2.30 = 56.5% instead of 44.8%.
Raising the turbine inlet temperature at the same r<sub>p</sub> does not change the ideal Brayton efficiency; it raises the net work and lowers the back work ratio.
w<sub>c</sub>/w<sub>t</sub> is the back work ratio, not the efficiency. η = w<sub>net</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>.
The Stirling efficiency equals Carnot only with a perfect regenerator. If the question says "without regenerator", add c<sub>v</sub>(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub>) to the heat input.
For maximum net work, T₂ = T₄ = √(T₁T₃). Examiners ask this as a derivation; show dw<sub>net</sub>/dx = 0, then solve for x.

quiz.q: List the four processes of the ideal Brayton cycle.
quiz.a: 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 constant-pressure heat addition, 3→4 isentropic expansion, 4→1 constant-pressure heat rejection.

quiz.q: What does the regenerator of a Stirling engine do?
quiz.a: It stores the heat given up by the gas during constant-volume cooling and returns it during constant-volume heating, so outside heat is needed only at T<sub>H</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is the pressure ratio, not a volume ratio, used for the Brayton cycle?
quiz.a: Each process happens in a separate steady-flow device at a fixed pressure level; the isentropic temperature ratios are set by the pressure ratio across the compressor and turbine.

quiz.q: Air enters a Brayton compressor at 300 K with r<sub>p</sub> = 4. Find T₂ and the ideal efficiency.
A Stirling engine with a perfect regenerator runs between 950 K and 320 K. Find its efficiency.
In the Brayton example, T₃ rises from 1200 K to 1400 K at r<sub>p</sub> = 8. What happens to η, w<sub>net</sub> and the back work ratio?
quiz.a: η stays 44.8%. T₄ = 1400/1.811 = 772.9 K, w<sub>t</sub> = 1.005 × 627.1 = 630.2 kJ/kg, w<sub>c</sub> = 244.7 kJ/kg, so w<sub>net</sub> = 385.5 kJ/kg (up from 295.6) and the back work ratio falls to 0.388.

quiz.q: Why does the efficiency of a Brayton cycle keep rising with r<sub>p</sub> while its net work falls past r<sub>p</sub> = 11.31 in the table?
quiz.a: η = 1 − T₁/T₂ grows as T₂ rises. But with T₃ fixed, a higher T₂ leaves less room for heat addition (T₃ − T₂ shrinks), so less heat goes in and less net work comes out even though a larger fraction of it becomes work.

beyond: Real gas turbines add intercooling, reheat and regeneration to the Brayton cycle, and combined-cycle power plants use the hot exhaust to raise steam for a Rankine cycle. A newer line of research uses supercritical carbon dioxide as the working fluid of a closed Brayton cycle, for compact turbines. Stirling engines are used for solar-dish power and in some submarines for air-independent propulsion. Search for "combined cycle gas turbine", "supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle" and "Stirling engine regenerator".
